evidence: Vulg. Lc. 10.5: In quamcumque domum intrāveritis
Plin. NH 9.86: omnia in domum conportat
terms.comment: The accusative answers “where to?” (quō?). With pōnere, put, Latin usually names where the thing ends up, in the ablative: in mēnsā pōnere, put on the table; its compounds (impōnere, īnferre) take in with the accusative.

terms.gloss: home, to the country; to Rome
evidence: Plaut. Men. 850b: Fuge domum, quantum potest.
terms.comment: Names of towns and small islands, domus and rūs take no preposition: domum īre, go home; rūs īre, go to the country. In domum is into a house, the building.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the accusative or in + accusative
evidence: Vulg. Lc. 10.5: In quamcumque domum intrāveritis
terms.comment: Latin often says “go into” with one verb: intrāre, introīre, ingredī (see enter); and “in” with a verb of motion is the adverb intrō (see inside).

phrases.latin: In quamcumque domum intrāveritis, prīmum dīcite: Pāx huic domuī.
phrases.english: Whatever house you go into, first say: Peace to this house.

phrases.latin: omnia in domum conportat, dein putāmina ērōsā carne ēgerit
phrases.english: it carries everything into its home, then eats the flesh and throws out the shells
Run home as fast as you can.

phrases.latin: accurrisse Rōmam et cum prīmō lūcī Pompōniī domum vēnisse dīcitur
phrases.english: he is said to have hurried to Rome and come to Pomponius’ house at first light
Let’s go in and have lunch.
